claim: RIPK3 normally signals to necroptosis by phosphorylating MLKL.
source: Receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 3 (RIPK3) normally signals to necroptosis by phosphorylating MLKL.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background knowledge about RIPK3 function.

claim: When cellular RIPK3 chaperone Hsp90/CDC37 level is low, RIPK3 signals to apoptosis.
source: We report here that when the cellular RIPK3 chaperone Hsp90/CDC37 level is low, RIPK3 also signals to apoptosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The apoptotic function of RIPK3 requires phosphorylation of serine 165/threonine 166 sites on its kinase activation loop.
source: The apoptotic function of RIPK3 requires phosphorylation of the serine 165/threonine 166 sites on its kinase activation loop, resulting in inactivation of RIPK3 kinase activity while gaining the ability to recruit RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8 to form a cytosolic caspase-activating complex, thereby triggering apoptosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: Phosphorylation of RIPK3 at serine 165/threonine 166 results in inactivation of RIPK3 kinase activity.
source: The apoptotic function of RIPK3 requires phosphorylation of the serine 165/threonine 166 sites on its kinase activation loop, resulting in inactivation of RIPK3 kinase activity while gaining the ability to recruit RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8 to form a cytosolic caspase-activating complex, thereby triggering apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by western blot data in Figure 3D showing loss of S227 phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphorylated RIPK3 gains the ability to recruit RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8 to form a cytosolic caspase-activating complex.
source: The apoptotic function of RIPK3 requires phosphorylation of the serine 165/threonine 166 sites on its kinase activation loop, resulting in inactivation of RIPK3 kinase activity while gaining the ability to recruit RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8 to form a cytosolic caspase-activating complex, thereby triggering apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figures 2A and 3H.

claim: PGF2α induces RIPK3 expression in luteal granulosa cells in the ovary.
source: We found that PGF2α induces RIPK3 expression in luteal granulosa cells in the ovary to cause luteal regression through this RIPK3-mediated apoptosis pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data in Figure 7.

claim: PGF2α causes luteal regression through RIPK3-mediated apoptosis pathway.
source: We found that PGF2α induces RIPK3 expression in luteal granulosa cells in the ovary to cause luteal regression through this RIPK3-mediated apoptosis pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7F-G showing cleaved caspase-3 in corpus luteum.

claim: Mice carrying homozygous phosphorylation-resistant RIPK3 S165A/T166A knockin mutations failed to respond to PGF2α.
source: Mice carrying homozygous phosphorylation-resistant RIPK3 S165A/T166A knockin mutations failed to respond to PGF2α but retained pro-necroptotic function
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 7F-G showing reduced cleaved caspase-3 in these mice.

claim: RIPK3 S165A/T166A knockin mice retained pro-necroptotic function.
source: Mice carrying homozygous phosphorylation-resistant RIPK3 S165A/T166A knockin mutations failed to respond to PGF2α but retained pro-necroptotic function
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H showing necroptosis response to TSZ.

claim: Mice with phospho-mimicking S165D/T166E homozygous knock-in mutation underwent spontaneous apoptosis in multiple RIPK3-expressing tissues.
source: whereas mice with phospho-mimicking S165D/T166E homozygous knock-in mutation underwent spontaneous apoptosis in multiple RIPK3-expressing tissues and died shortly after birth.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by histology and cleaved caspase-3 staining in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Mice with phospho-mimicking S165D/T166E homozygous knock-in mutation died shortly after birth.
source: whereas mice with phospho-mimicking S165D/T166E homozygous knock-in mutation underwent spontaneous apoptosis in multiple RIPK3-expressing tissues and died shortly after birth.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by survival curve in Figure 5C showing death within 1 month.

claim: RIPK3 signals to either necroptosis or apoptosis depending on its serine 165/threonine 166 phosphorylation status.
source: Thus, RIPK3 signals to either necroptosis or apoptosis depending on its serine 165/threonine 166 phosphorylation status.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Apoptosis is executed by intracellular caspases, particularly caspase-3.
source: Apoptosis is executed by intracellular caspases, particularly caspase-3, whose cleavage of several intracellular substrates gives rise to characteristic features of apoptotic cell death.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction with citations (Elmore, 2007; Fink and Cookson, 2005; Kroemer et al., 2009; Wallach et al., 2016).

claim: Caspase-3 is activated by upstream caspase-8 or caspase-9.
source: Caspase-3 is activated by upstream caspase-8 or caspase-9, which are known to be activated respectively by being part of plasma membrane-associated death-inducing signaling complexes induced by the TNF family of cytokines, or being part of the cytosolic apoptosome, which is formed as a result of cytochrome c release from mitochondria (Elmore, 2007; Li et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Cells that die by apoptosis maintain their plasma membrane integrity and break down into small vesicles phagocytosed by macrophages.
source: Cells that die by apoptosis maintain their plasma membrane integrity and break down into small vesicles phagocytosed by macrophages (Elmore, 2007; Kroemer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Cells that die by regulated necrosis are executed by membrane-disrupting proteins.
source: Cells that die by regulated necrosis are executed by membrane-disrupting proteins that, when activated, translocate from the cytosol to the plasma membrane and disperse cellular contents into the cell surroundings.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: Regulated necrosis is often associated with inflammatory response.
source: This process is often associated with inflammatory response (Christofferson and Yuan, 2010; Vandenabeele et al., 2010; Wallach et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Necroptosis is executed by MLKL.
source: One form of regulated necrosis, necroptosis, is executed by a pseudokinase, namely mixed lineage kinase-domain protein, MLKL (Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: MLKL is a substrate of RIPK3.
source: MLKL is a substrate of receptor-interacting kinase RIPK3, which becomes activated either by (1) the TNF family of cytokines through a related kinase RIPK1 that interacts with RIPK3 through a RIP homotypic interaction motif (RHIM) domain or (2) by other RHIM domain-containing proteins, such as TRIF or ZBP1/DAI, that relay necroptotic signals from Toll-like receptors or intracellular Z-RNA, respectively (Cho et al., 2009; Degterev et al., 2008; He et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2012; Upton et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Active RIPK3 phosphorylates MLKL at serine 357/threonine 358 sites to induce oligomerization and translocation to the plasma membrane.
source: Active RIPK3 phosphorylates MLKL at serine 357/threonine 358 (human origin) sites to induce oligomerization and translocation from the cytosol to the plasma membrane and cause loss of membrane integrity (Cai et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: A kinase-dead mutant RIPK3 D161N spontaneously causes host cells to undergo apoptosis.
source: Surprisingly, a kinase-dead mutant RIPK3, D161N, spontaneously causes host cells to undergo apoptosis, resulting in embryonic lethality in mice bearing such homozygous mutation (Newton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citation.

claim: Mice homozygous with RIPK3 D161N mutation show embryonic lethality.
source: Surprisingly, a kinase-dead mutant RIPK3, D161N, spontaneously causes host cells to undergo apoptosis, resulting in embryonic lethality in mice bearing such homozygous mutation (Newton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citation.

claim: Mice homozygous with K51A RIPK3 mutation do not show spontaneous apoptosis phenotype.
source: On the other hand, mice homozygous with another kinase-dead mutant, K51A RIPK3, do not share this phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: Cells with K51A RIPK3 mutation are sensitive to apoptosis induction when treated with small-molecule RIPK3 inhibitors.
source: However, cells that harbor this mutation are sensitive to apoptosis induction when treated with several small-molecule RIPK3 inhibitors that bind to its ATP-binding pocket (Mandal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citation.

claim: Apoptosis has essential functions during animal development and maintaining cell homeostasis in adults.
source: Apoptosis has essential functions during animal development and maintaining cell homeostasis in adults (Elmore, 2007; Fink and Cookson, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Necroptosis functions include antiviral infections, tissue damage response, and male reproductive system aging.
source: Necroptosis functions include antiviral infections, tissue damage response, and male reproductive system aging (Cho et al., 2009; He and Wang, 2018; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: One important physiological function of apoptosis in adult mammals is the development and function of the ovary.
source: One of the important physiological functions of apoptosis in adult mammals is the development and function of the ovary (Perez et al., 1997; Rimon-Dahari et al., 2016; Rolaki et al., 2005; Tilly, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Most eggs within primordial follicles fail to develop and undergo atresia driven by apoptosis.
source: From the neonatal stage to sex maturation, most eggs within primordial follicles fail to develop and undergo a process called atresia – a process driven by apoptosis of the egg and surrounding granulosa cells (Rimon-Dahari et al., 2016; Tilly and Sinclair, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: After sex maturation, follicles develop from primordial to primary and secondary follicles accompanied by proliferation of surrounding granulosa and theca cells.
source: After sex maturation, follicles develop from primordial to primary and secondary follicles accompanied by the proliferation of surrounding granulosa and theca cells (Rimon-Dahari et al., 2016; Sánchez and Smitz, 2012; Tilly and Sinclair, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: After egg release during ovulation, the remaining granulosa and theca cells become progesterone-producing corpus luteum.
source: After egg release from the follicle during ovulation, the remaining granulosa and theca cells become progesterone-producing sources, namely corpus luteum, which is easily recognizable under a microscope (Rolaki et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: If the egg is unfertilized, the corpus luteum dies through apoptosis and becomes corpus albicans.
source: If the egg is unfertilized, the corpus luteum dies through apoptosis and becomes corpus albicans, a scar tissue with a mixture of cell debris, macrophages, type I collagen, and fibroblasts, and is light in color compared to the luteum.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: Luteal involution stops the production of progesterone and triggers another cycle of ovulation.
source: Such a process stops the production of progesterone and triggers another cycle of ovulation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: When mammals age, their follicles and corpora lutea are gradually lost.
source: When mammals age, their follicles and corpora lutea are gradually lost, and the ovary eventually becomes a corpus albicans-filled organ that ceases to produce eggs and hormones (Perheentupa and Huhtaniemi, 2009; Tilly, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Ectopic expression of RIPK3 in MCF7 cells caused cell death.
source: Surprisingly, we found that simple expression of RIPK3 in MCF7 or KGN cells caused cell death (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 1A.

claim: Ectopic expression of RIPK3 in KGN cells caused cell death.
source: Surprisingly, we found that simple expression of RIPK3 in MCF7 or KGN cells caused cell death (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopic expression of RIPK3 in HeLa cells did not affect cell viability.
source: whereas the ectopic expression of RIPK3 in HeLa cells did not affect cell viability, similar to previous studies (Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by cell viability data in Figure 1A.

claim: RIPK3-expressing MCF7 and KGN cells did not undergo necroptosis when treated with TSZ.
source: Moreover, these RIPK3-expressing MCF7 and KGN cells did not undergo necroptosis when we treated the cells with TSZ (TNFα [T], a Smac mimetic [S], and a pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-fml [Z]), whereas such treatment caused robust necroptosis in RIPK3-expressing HeLa cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 1B.

claim: TSZ treatment caused robust necroptosis in RIPK3-expressing HeLa cells.
source: Moreover, these RIPK3-expressing MCF7 and KGN cells did not undergo necroptosis when we treated the cells with TSZ (TNFα [T], a Smac mimetic [S], and a pan-caspase inhibitor Z-VAD-fml [Z]), whereas such treatment caused robust necroptosis in RIPK3-expressing HeLa cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 1B.

claim: Cell death induced by RIPK3 in MCF7 cells could be blocked by caspase inhibitor z-VAD-fmk.
source: Cell death induced by Dox could be blocked by caspase inhibitor z-VAD-fmk (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 1C.

claim: Cell death induced by RIPK3 in MCF7 cells could not be blocked by MLKL inhibitor NSA.
source: but not by MLKL inhibitor NSA, nor RIPK1 kinase inhibitor RIPA-56 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 1C.

claim: Cell death induced by RIPK3 in MCF7 cells could not be blocked by RIPK1 kinase inhibitor RIPA-56.
source: but not by MLKL inhibitor NSA, nor RIPK1 kinase inhibitor RIPA-56 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 1C.

claim: RIPK3-mediated cell death in MCF7 cells was apoptotic.
source: indicating that the observed RIPK3-mediated cell death was apoptotic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inhibitor data showing z-VAD blocks death but NSA and RIPA-56 do not.

claim: RIPK3-mediated apoptosis did not signal through the classic intrinsic mitochondrial pathway.
source: However, this form of apoptosis did not signal through the classic intrinsic mitochondrial pathway as the loss of cell viability through this pathway could not be blocked by caspase inhibitors
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that caspase inhibitors block the death.

claim: Kinase-dead mutant RIPK3(K50A) did not cause cell death in MCF7 cells.
source: we expressed a previously reported kinase-dead mutant (K50A) of RIPK3 in MCF7 cells and found that this kinase-dead mutant RIPK3(K50A) did not cause cell death (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 1D.

claim: Expression of kinase-dead mutant RIPK3(K50A) plus RIPK3 kinase inhibitor GSK'872 resulted in robust apoptosis.
source: Interestingly, the expression of this kinase-dead mutant RIPK3(K50A) plus RIPK3 kinase inhibitor GSK'872 resulted in robust apoptosis, similar to what was described by Mandal et al. (Figure 1D; Mandal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 1D and cited prior work.

claim: Mutations at the RHIM domain of RIPK3 caused complete loss of cell death induction.
source: Moreover, the mutations at the RHIM domain of RIPK3 known to disrupt RHIM-RHIM interaction also caused complete loss of cell death induction, indicating that RHIM domain interaction, possibly with another RHIM domain-containing protein, is required for apoptotic induction by RIPK3 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 1D.

claim: RHIM domain interaction is required for apoptotic induction by RIPK3.
source: Moreover, the mutations at the RHIM domain of RIPK3 known to disrupt RHIM-RHIM interaction also caused complete loss of cell death induction, indicating that RHIM domain interaction, possibly with another RHIM domain-containing protein, is required for apoptotic induction by RIPK3 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the RHIM mutant data.

claim: RIPK1, caspase-8, and FADD were co-immunoprecipitated with RIPK3.
source: We therefore immunoprecipitated the Flag-tagged RIPK3 and probed the immune-precipitate with antibodies against RIPK1, caspase-8, and FADD. Indeed, all three proteins were co-immunoprecipitated with RIPK3.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2A.

claim: The amount of RIPK1 and caspase-8 associated with RIPK3 increased when a caspase inhibitor was present.
source: The amount of RIPK1 and caspase-8 associated with RIPK3 increased when a caspase inhibitor was present, indicating the complex had increased stability when caspase-8 activity was blocked, presumably by preventing caspase-8-mediated cleavage of RIPK1, which serves as an adaptor protein between RIPK3 (through the RHIM domain) and FADD (through the DEAD domain) (Figure 2A; Mandal et al., 2014; Newton et al., 2014; Sun et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2A.

claim: Knocking out RIPK1 gene in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 cells blocked cell death upon Dox addition.
source: When we used the CRISPR/Cas9 to knock out either RIPK1, caspase-8, or FADD gene in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 cells, we found that cell death upon addition of Dox was blocked entirely (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 2B.

claim: Knocking out caspase-8 gene in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 cells blocked cell death upon Dox addition.
source: When we used the CRISPR/Cas9 to knock out either RIPK1, caspase-8, or FADD gene in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 cells, we found that cell death upon addition of Dox was blocked entirely (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 2C.

claim: Knocking out FADD gene in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 cells blocked cell death upon Dox addition.
source: When we used the CRISPR/Cas9 to knock out either RIPK1, caspase-8, or FADD gene in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 cells, we found that cell death upon addition of Dox was blocked entirely (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 2D.

claim: Knocking out the cFLIP gene did not block RIPK3-induced apoptosis in MCF7 cells but rather enhanced it.
source: Interestingly, different from the previous report (Mandal et al., 2014), knocking out the cFLIP gene did not block RIPK3-induced apoptosis in MCF7 cells but rather enhanced it (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 2E.

claim: Serine 164 and threonine 165 of RIPK3 were specifically phosphorylated in MCF7 cells but not in HeLa cells.
source: We found two amino acid residues at the activation loop of the RIPK3 kinase domain, serine 164 and threonine 165, that were specifically phosphorylated in MCF7 cells but not in HeLa cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 3A.

claim: A monoclonal antibody against phospho-S164/T165 peptide only recognized RIPK3 protein expressed in KGN or MCF7 cells but not in HeLa cells.
source: This phospho-specific antibody only recognized RIPK3 protein expressed in KGN or MCF7 cells but not in HeLa cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 3B.

claim: The phosphorylation-resistant S164A/T165A mutant protein could only be recognized by the anti-RIPK3 antibody but not the anti-phospho-S164/T165 antibody.
source: The phosphorylation-resistant S164A/T165A mutant protein could only be recognized by the anti-RIPK3 antibody but not the anti-phospho-S614/T165 antibody.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Expression of kinase-dead mutants RIPK3 D160N and RIPK3 K50A failed to generate the phospho-S164/T165 signal.
source: Additionally, the expression of two kinase-dead mutants RIPK3 D160N and RIPK3 K50A (equivalent of mouse D161N and K51A, respectively) failed to generate the phospho-S164/T165 signal (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RIPK3-induced apoptosis in KGN and MCF7 cells requires serine 164/threonine 165 phosphorylation of RIPK3.
source: Therefore, the RIPK3-induced apoptosis in KGN and MCF7 cells requires serine 164/threonine 165 phosphorylation of RIPK3, an event dependent on its intact kinase domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinase-dead mutant data.

claim: Serine 164/threonine 165 phosphorylation of RIPK3 is dependent on its intact kinase domain.
source: Therefore, the RIPK3-induced apoptosis in KGN and MCF7 cells requires serine 164/threonine 165 phosphorylation of RIPK3, an event dependent on its intact kinase domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinase-dead mutant data showing no phosphorylation.

claim: The serine 164/threonine 165 region of RIPK3 is conserved among mammalian species.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, this region is conserved with no changes from amino acid residues 160–174 among RIPK3s from human, chimpanzee, rat, mouse, and bovine origin (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by sequence alignment in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Mouse RIPK3(S165D/T166E) failed to auto-phosphorylate the serine 232 site.
source: The corresponding phospho-mimic mutations of mouse RIPK3(S165D/T166E), like RIPK3(D161N) kinase-dead mutants (Newton et al., 2014), failed to auto-phosphorylate the serine 232 site, the equivalent of the human serine 227 site (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Phospho-mimic RIPK3 S164D/T165E mutations failed to auto-phosphorylate the serine 227 site.
source: After transiently transfecting the cDNA of mutant RIPK3 in human embryonic kidney 293T cells, we observed that RIPK3 bearing phospho-mimic S164D/T165E mutations failed to auto-phosphorylate the serine 227 site, similar to the kinase-dead mutant D160N, whereas wild-type RIPK3 readily phosphorylated serine 227 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 3D.

claim: Wild-type RIPK3 readily phosphorylated serine 227.
source: After transiently transfecting the cDNA of mutant RIPK3 in human embryonic kidney 293T cells, we observed that RIPK3 bearing phospho-mimic S164D/T165E mutations failed to auto-phosphorylate the serine 227 site, similar to the kinase-dead mutant D160N, whereas wild-type RIPK3 readily phosphorylated serine 227 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 3D.

claim: Phospho-mimic mutations S164D/T165E increased apoptosis in MCF7 and KGN cells compared to wild-type RIPK3.
source: As shown in Figure 3E, F, introducing phospho-mimic mutations S164D/T165E increased apoptosis in MCF7 and KGN cells compared to wild-type RIPK3
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 3E, F.

claim: Phosphorylation-resistant mutant S164A/T165A lost the ability to induce apoptosis.
source: whereas the phosphorylation-resistant mutant S164A/T165A lost the ability to induce apoptosis, similar to the RHIM domain mutant.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 3E, F.

claim: Phospho-mimic mutant S164D/T165E gained the ability to induce apoptosis in HeLa cells.
source: Remarkably, in HeLa cells, the phospho-mimic mutant S164D/T165E gained the ability to induce apoptosis similar to the kinase-dead mutant D160N (Figure 3G)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 3G.

claim: Phospho-mimic mutant S164D/T165E was no longer able to induce necroptosis in HeLa cells when treated with TSZ.
source: Since the phospho-mimic mutations inactivate RIPK3 kinase activity (Figure 3D), this S164D/T165E mutant was no longer able to induce necroptosis in HeLa cells when treated with necroptosis stimuli TSZ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Phosphorylation-resistant mutant S164A/T165A still allowed HeLa cells to respond to necroptosis induction.
source: The phosphorylation-resistant mutant S164A/T165A still allowed HeLa cells to respond to necroptosis induction, though the apoptosis-inducing function was lost when the mutant RIPK3 was expressed in KGN and MCF7 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Phospho-mimic S164E, but not T165E, mutant lost necroptosis responsiveness and gained the ability to induce apoptosis in HeLa cells.
source: The phospho-mimic S164E, but not T165E, mutant lost necroptosis responsiveness and gained the ability to induce apoptosis in HeLa cells
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Phosphorylation-resistant S164A, but not T165A, lost its apoptosis-inducing activity in KGN and MCF7 cells.
source: while phosphorylation-resistant S164A, but not T165A, lost its apoptosis-inducing activity in KGN and MCF7 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-G.

claim: RIPK3 auto-phosphorylation on the serine S164 site is a critical event that inactivates RIPK3 kinase activity while gaining apoptosis-inducing activity.
source: Together, these results indicated that RIPK3 auto-phosphorylation on the serine S164 site is a critical event that inactivates RIPK3 kinase activity while gaining apoptosis-inducing activity in KGN and MCF7 cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the single-site mutant data.

claim: Phospho-mimic RIPK3 (S164D/T165E) showed robust binding with RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8.
source: In contrast, two kinase-dead mutants, either the artificial D160N or phospho-mimic S164D/T165E, showed robust binding with RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8 (Figure 3H, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3H.

claim: Kinase-dead mutant D160N showed robust binding with RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8.
source: In contrast, two kinase-dead mutants, either the artificial D160N or phospho-mimic S164D/T165E, showed robust binding with RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8 (Figure 3H, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3H.

claim: Phosphorylation-resistant mutant S164A/T165A lost the ability to bind with RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8.
source: Consistent with the cell death result, the phosphorylation-resistant mutant S164A/T165A lost the ability to bind with RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3I.

claim: Phospho-mimic S164E mutant expressed in HeLa cells was found to associate with RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8.
source: Consistent with the finding that the serine 164 phosphorylation is most critical for RIPK3 apoptosis-inducing activity, the phospho-mimic S164E mutant expressed in HeLa cells was found to associate with RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8, as did the S164D/T165E double mutation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H, lane 4)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: T165E alone could not bind to RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8.
source: whereas T165E alone could not bind to these proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H, lane 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: RIPK3 auto-phosphorylation on serine S164 allows RIPK3 to recruit RIPK1 to form the RIPK3/RIPK1/FADD/caspase-8 complex.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that RIPK3 auto-phosphorylation on serine S164 allows RIPK3 to recruit RIPK1 to form the RIPK3/RIPK1/FADD/caspase-8 complex, in which caspase-8 is activated to drive apoptosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the binding and cell death data.

claim: RIPK3 needs to be correctly folded with the aid of Hsp90 and CDC37 chaperone to signal to necroptosis.
source: We have previously observed that in order for RIPK3 to signal to necroptosis the protein needs to be correctly folded with the aid of a molecular chaperone consisting of Hsp90 and CDC37 (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citation.

claim: The level of Hsp90/CDC37 was higher in HT29 and HeLa cells compared to MCF7 and KGN cells.
source: In HT29 and HeLa cells in which RIPK3 signals primarily to necroptosis, we observed that the level of Hsp90/CDC37 was higher compared to MCF7 and KGN cells, where RIPK3 predominantly causes apoptosis (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 4A.

claim: Hsp90 inhibitor 17AAG potently blocked necroptosis induced by TSZ in HeLa-RIPK3 cells.
source: Indeed, a human Hsp90 inhibitor 17AAG potently blocked necroptosis induced by TSZ in HeLa-RIPK3 cells
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 4B.

claim: 17AAG did not block RIPK3-induced apoptosis in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 or KGN/TO-RIPK3 cells.
source: whereas 17AAG did not block RIPK3-induced apoptosis in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 or KGN/TO-RIPK3 cells (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 4B, C.

claim: Knocking down Hsp90 using shRNA switched the cellular necroptosis response to apoptosis.
source: When we knocked down Hsp90 using shRNA or inhibits Hsp90 using 17AAG, after Dox induce RIPK3 expression, we saw the switch of the cellular necroptosis response to apoptosis (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Serine 164/threonine 165 phosphorylation of RIPK3 occurred after the inhibition of Hsp90.
source: Consistently, the serine 164/threonine 165 phosphorylation of RIPK3 also occurred after the inhibition of Hsp90 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 4E.

claim: Ectopic expression of Hsp90 and CDC37 in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 cells prevented serine 164/threonine 165 phosphorylation of RIPK3.

claim: Ectopic expression of Hsp90 and CDC37 in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 cells caused RIPK3-mediated apoptosis induction to mostly cease.
source: Reciprocally, when Hsp90 and CDC37 were ectopically expressed in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 cells to a level matched or exceeding that in HeLa cells, the serine 164/threonine 165 phosphorylation of RIPK3 no longer occurred, and RIPK3-mediated apoptosis induction mostly ceased (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 4F.

claim: When Hsp90 inhibitor 17AAG was present during RIPK3 induction in HeLa/TO-RIPK3 cells, RIPK3 formed a complex with RIPK1, FADD, and caspase-8.

claim: Using higher concentrations of 17AAG blocked TSZ-induced necroptosis in L929 cells.

claim: Knocking down Hsp90 or inhibiting Hsp90 in L929 (Ripk3-/-)/TO-RIPK3 cells switched the cellular necroptosis response to apoptosis.

claim: Serine 165/threonine 166 phosphorylation of RIPK3 occurred after the inhibition of Hsp90 in mouse cells.
source: The serine 165/threonine 166 phosphorylation of RIPK3 also occurred after the inhibition of Hsp90 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Hsp90/CDC37-determined, RIPK3 serine 164/threonine 165 phosphorylation-driven apoptosis is conserved between human and mouse cells.
source: These results indicated that the observed Hsp90/CDC37-determined, RIPK3 serine 164/threonine 165 phosphorylation-driven apoptosis is conserved between human and mouse cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mouse cell data.

claim: RIPK3 formed diffused puncta within the cytosol in HeLa/TO-RIPK3 cells treated with Dox plus TSZ.
source: Indeed, when the HeLa/TO-RIPK3 cells were treated with Dox plus TSZ, we observed expressed RIPK3 in diffused puncta in the cytosol (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).

claim: RIPK3 formed a high order of structures distinct from diffused punctae in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 and KGN/TO-RIPK3 cells.
source: Interestingly, when we performed a similar analysis of RIPK3 distribution in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 and KGN/TO-RIPK3 cells, the RIPK3 formed a high order of structures distinct from the diffused punctae in HeLa or HT29 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).

claim: Phospho-S164/T165-RIPK3 signal appeared co-localized with RIPK3 in MCF7 cells.
source: Furthermore, the phospho-S164/T165-RIPK3 signal appeared co-localized with RIPK3 in MCF7 cells, but no such signal was seen in HeLa cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Formation of high-order structures and appearance of phospho-S164/T165-RIPK3 signal were not affected when RIPK1, caspase-8, or FADD genes were knocked out.
source: The formation of these high-order structures and the appearance of the phospho-S164/T165-RIPK3 signal were not affected when RIPK1, caspase-8, or FADD genes were knocked out (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D, E)

claim: RIPK3 is responsible for forming high-order intracellular structures.
source: indicating that it was RIPK3, not its downstream apoptotic effectors, that was responsible for forming these high-order intracellular structures.
evidence: This is an inference based on the knockout data.

claim: Treatment of HeLa/TO-RIPK3 cells with Dox plus Hsp90 inhibitor 17AAG switched diffused punctae of RIPK3 to high-order structure.
source: To test whether this high-order structure of RIPK3 is associated with its ability to induce apoptosis, we treated the HeLa/TO-RIPK3 cells with Dox plus the Hsp90 inhibitor 17AAG and found that the diffused punctae of RIPK3 were now switched to the high-order structure (Figure 4I).

claim: Ectopic overexpression of Hsp90 and CDC37 in MCF7/TO-RIPK3 cells caused the high-order structure of RIPK3 to become diffused punctae.

evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4J.

claim: RIPK3 forms distinctive cellular structures when signaling to apoptosis or necroptosis, depending on the chaperone Hsp90/CDC37.
source: These findings collectively indicated that RIPK3 forms distinctive cellular structures when signaling to apoptosis or necroptosis, depending on the chaperone Hsp90/CDC37.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the structural and chaperone data.

claim: Ripk3S165A-T166A/S165A-T166A homozygous mice were viable and appeared normal.

claim: Ripk3S165D-T166E/S165D-T166E homozygous mice are smaller in size.

claim: Brain, cerebellum, heart, and liver appeared normal in Ripk3S165D-T166E/S165D-T166E mice.
source: Anatomical analysis of these Ripk3S165D-T166E/S165D-T166E mice showed abnormal large intestine, small intestine, lung, spleen, and kidney, while other major organs, including brain, cerebellum, heart, and liver, appeared normal (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).

claim: Significantly increased apoptosis was revealed in the large intestine, small intestine, lung, and spleen of Ripk3S165D-T166E/S165D-T166E mice.

claim: There is a threshold above which the RIPK3 S165D/T166E protein becomes lethal.

evidence: This is speculation based on the heterozygous viability.

evidence: This is speculation based on the heterozygous viability.

claim: BMDM from Ripk3S165A-T166A/S165A-T166A mice readily underwent necroptosis when treated with TSZ.

evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cell viability data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Caspase inhibitor z-VAD-fmk was needed to prevent spontaneous cell death when culturing BMDM from Ripk3S165D-T166E/S165D-T166E mice.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: RIPK3 expression levels in the ovary followed a reversed bell curve pattern through the lifetime of mice.
source: Among all RIPK3-expressing tissues, RIPK3 expression levels in the ovary were the most notable, following a reversed bell curve pattern through the lifetime of the mice (Figure 6A).

claim: In early life and young adulthood, RIPK3 expression was restricted to the follicle granular cells around the egg.
source: In early life and young adulthood, RIPK3 expression was restricted to the follicle granular cells around the egg (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6B.

claim: In later life, RIPK3 protein starts to appear in the corpus luteum and albican.
source: In later life, RIPK3 protein starts to appear in the corpus luteum and albican (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6B.

claim: The second wave of RIPK3 expression coincides with the elevation of prostaglandin F2alpha (PGF2α).
source: The second wave of expression coincides with the elevation of prostaglandin F2alpha (PGF2α), which has been reported to have a role in apoptosis induction during luteal involution (Parkening et al., 1985).
evidence: This is stated in the Results with citation.

claim: PGF2α levels in the mouse ovary showed a significant age-dependent increase as mice aged from 4 months to 10 and 16 months.

evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ELISA data in Figure 6C.

claim: PTGFR signal was primarily located in corpus lutea and corpus albicans but not in the follicles.
source: Moreover, when we co-stained 12-month-old RIPK3-Flag knock-in ovaries with anti-Flag and prostaglandin F receptor (PTGFR), we noticed that the PTGFR signal was primarily located in corpus lutea and corpus albicans but not in the follicles and co-localized with that of RIPK3 (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6D.

claim: PTGFR co-localized with RIPK3 in corpus lutea and corpus albicans.
source: Moreover, when we co-stained 12-month-old RIPK3-Flag knock-in ovaries with anti-Flag and prostaglandin F receptor (PTGFR), we noticed that the PTGFR signal was primarily located in corpus lutea and corpus albicans but not in the follicles and co-localized with that of RIPK3 (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6D.

claim: No phosphorylation signal was found in young (2-month-old) ovaries despite RIPK3 protein being readily detectable.
source: We found no phosphorylation signal in young (2-month-old) ovaries, despite the RIPK3 protein band being readily detectable (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 6E.

claim: Phospho-S164/T165 signal began to appear at 4 months and gradually increased when mice advanced in age.
source: The signal began to appear at 4 months and gradually increased when mice advanced in age (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 6E.

claim: There was minimal phospho-RIPK3 signal in the young (4-month-old) ovary.
source: Consistent with the western blotting, there was minimal signal in the young (4-month-old) ovary.
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6F.

claim: There were patches of phospho-RIPK3 signal in 8-month-old corpus luteum and albican.
source: There were patches of signal in 8-month-old corpus luteum and albican, and the signal became prominent and clustered in the corpus albicans in 12-month-old ovary (Figure 6F, middle panels).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6F.

claim: Phospho-RIPK3 signal became prominent and clustered in the corpus albicans in 12-month-old ovary.
source: There were patches of signal in 8-month-old corpus luteum and albican, and the signal became prominent and clustered in the corpus albicans in 12-month-old ovary (Figure 6F, middle panels).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6F.

claim: No phospho-RIPK3 signal was seen in 12-month-old ovaries of RIPK3 knockout mice.
source: In contrast, no such phospho-RIPK3 signal was seen in 12-month-old ovaries of RIPK3 knockout mice, further confirming the specificity of this monoclonal antibody (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6F.

claim: Both Hsp90 and CDC37 antibodies stained follicle granulosa much more strongly than corpus lutea and albicans.
source: Both antibodies stained follicle granulosa much more strongly than corpus lutea and albicans, whereas RIPK3 staining signal was at a similar level in both, indicating that the relative level of Hsp90/CDC37 vs. RIPK3 is higher in follicles than corpus lutea and albicans (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The relative level of Hsp90/CDC37 vs. RIPK3 is higher in follicles than corpus lutea and albicans.
source: Both antibodies stained follicle granulosa much more strongly than corpus lutea and albicans, whereas RIPK3 staining signal was at a similar level in both, indicating that the relative level of Hsp90/CDC37 vs. RIPK3 is higher in follicles than corpus lutea and albicans (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the staining intensity data.

claim: RIPK3-induced apoptosis only happens in aged corpus lutea and albicans might be due to relative lower levels of Hsp90/CDC37 chaperone in these regions of the ovary.
source: Collectively, these results suggested that RIPK3-induced apoptosis only happens in aged corpus lutea and albicans might be due to relative lower levels of Hsp90/CDC37 chaperone in these regions of the ovary.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the chaperone level data.

claim: PGF2α is known to stimulate the Raf/MEK1/mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling pathway to induce luteal regression.
source: PGF2α is known to stimulate the Raf/MEK1/mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling pathway to induce luteal regression (Chen et al., 1998; Rolaki et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2003; Yadav et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Knockout caspase-3 blocks PGF2α-induced regression of the corpus luteum in mice.
source: In mice, knockout caspase-3 blocks PGF2α-induced regression of the corpus luteum (Carambula et al., 2002; Carambula et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citations.

claim: Treatment with synthetic PGF2α analog dinoprost tromethamine (DT) caused time- and dose-dependent induction of RIPK3 protein in primary granulosa lutein cells.
source: To test if PGF2α could directly induce RIPK3 expression, we isolated primary granulosa lutein cells from young (3-month-old) mouse ovaries and treated them with a synthetic PGF2α analog dinoprost tromethamine (DT) (Chebel et al., 2007). We then observed the time- and dose-dependent induction of RIPK3 protein, a pattern that overlapped with the appearance of phospho-ERK/MEK signal, an indication of PGF2 receptor activation (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 7A, B.

claim: RIPK3 induction pattern overlapped with the appearance of phospho-ERK/MEK signal.
source: We then observed the time- and dose-dependent induction of RIPK3 protein, a pattern that overlapped with the appearance of phospho-ERK/MEK signal, an indication of PGF2 receptor activation (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 7A, B.

claim: Addition of MEK kinase inhibitors PD-98059 or U0126 blocked RIPK3 induction.
source: The addition of two MEK kinase inhibitors PD-98059 or U0126 blocked RIPK3 induction, confirming that the RIPK3 induction by PGF2α was indeed through the MEK pathway (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RIPK3 induction by PGF2α was through the MEK pathway.
source: The addition of two MEK kinase inhibitors PD-98059 or U0126 blocked RIPK3 induction, confirming that the RIPK3 induction by PGF2α was indeed through the MEK pathway (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MEK inhibitor data.

claim: DT-induced RIPK3 was phosphorylated at its serine 165/threonine 166 sites.
source: Importantly, the DT-induced RIPK3 was phosphorylated at its serine 165/threonine 166 sites, and the treated cells were undergoing apoptosis, as indicated by the presence of active caspase-3 (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 7C.

claim: DT-treated primary granulosa lutein cells were undergoing apoptosis, as indicated by the presence of active caspase-3.
source: Importantly, the DT-induced RIPK3 was phosphorylated at its serine 165/threonine 166 sites, and the treated cells were undergoing apoptosis, as indicated by the presence of active caspase-3 (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 7C.

claim: Primary granulosa lutein cells isolated from RIPK3 knockout mice failed to respond to PGF2α to activate caspase-3.
source: Consistent with the notion that apoptosis induced by PGF2α is RIPK3 dependent, the primary granulosa lutein cells isolated from the RIPK3 knockout mice failed to respond to PGF2α activate caspase-3 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 7C.

claim: DT treatment induced the elevation of RIPK3 protein in corpus lutea of wild-type ovaries.
source: The hyper-ovulation induced by gonadotropins generated multiple corpus lutea in the ovaries of these young mice (Figure 7D). The subsequent DT treatment induced the elevation of RIPK3 protein in their corpus lutea, and the induced RIPK3 was phosphorylated at the serine 164/threonine 165 sites (Figure 7D, E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data in Figure 7D, E.

claim: Induced RIPK3 was phosphorylated at the serine 164/threonine 165 sites in corpus lutea after DT treatment.
source: The subsequent DT treatment induced the elevation of RIPK3 protein in their corpus lutea, and the induced RIPK3 was phosphorylated at the serine 164/threonine 165 sites (Figure 7D, E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 7E.

claim: Treatment of DT caused active caspase-3 signal to appear in the corpus lutea of wild-type ovaries.
source: Moreover, the treatment of DT caused active caspase-3 signal to appear in the corpus lutea of wild-type ovaries (Figure 7F, G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 7F, G.

claim: Mice with PTGFR gene knocked out failed to elevate the RIPK3 level in response to PGF2α.
source: Mice with their PTGFR gene knocked out failed to elevate the RIPK3 level in response to PGF2α (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, D, Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 7E.

claim: DT treatment induced the elevation of phosphorylation-resistant RIPK3(S165A/T166A) protein in the ovaries of Ripk3S165A-T166A/S165A-T166A knock-in mice to the same level as wild-type RIPK3 protein.
source: Although DT treatment induced the elevation of phosphorylation-resistant RIPK3(S165A/T166A) protein in the ovaries of Ripk3S165A-T166A/S165A-T166A knock-in mice to the same level as wild-type RIPK3 protein (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Significantly less active caspase-3 signal was observed in ovaries of Ripk3-/-, Fadd-/-/Mlkl-/-, or Ptgfr-/- mice after DT treatment.
source: significantly less active caspase-3 signal was observed in these ovaries, similar to the ovaries of Ripk3-/-, Fadd-/-/Mlkl-/-, or Ptgfr-/- mice, confirming that the observed DT-induced apoptosis in luteal cells was through the RIPK3/FADD-mediated apoptosis pathway triggered by the phosphorylation of serine 165/threonine 166 sites (Figure 7F, G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 7F, G.

claim: DT-induced apoptosis in luteal cells was through the RIPK3/FADD-mediated apoptosis pathway triggered by the phosphorylation of serine 165/threonine 166 sites.
source: significantly less active caspase-3 signal was observed in these ovaries, similar to the ovaries of Ripk3-/-, Fadd-/-/Mlkl-/-, or Ptgfr-/- mice, confirming that the observed DT-induced apoptosis in luteal cells was through the RIPK3/FADD-mediated apoptosis pathway triggered by the phosphorylation of serine 165/threonine 166 sites (Figure 7F, G).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic knockout data.

claim: Most of the positive signals for active caspase-3 and phospho-S165/T166 RIPK3 were overlapping in ovaries.
source: We further co-stained the ovaries with antibodies against active caspase-3 and phospho-S165/T166 RIPK3 and found that most of the positive signals were overlapping (Figure 7H)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 7H.

claim: Serine 165/threonine 166 phosphorylated RIPK3 activates apoptosis in corpus luteum, triggered by PGF2α.
source: indicating that serine 165/threonine 166 phosphorylated RIPK3 activates apoptosis in corpus luteum, triggered by PGF2α.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the co-staining data.

claim: There was more active caspase-3 in Ripk3-/- and Ripk3S165A-T166A/S165A-T166A ovaries than in Fadd-/-/Mlkl-/- ovaries.
source: Interestingly, although significantly lower overall, there was more active caspase-3 in Ripk3-/- and Ripk3S165A-T166A/S165A-T166A ovaries than in Fadd-/-/Mlkl-/- ovaries
evidence: This is stated in the Results and supported by data in Figure 7G.

claim: There might be a redundant RIPK3-independent but FADD-dependent apoptosis pathway that also functions in resolving the corpus luteum.
source: suggesting that there might be a redundant RIPK3-independent but FADD-dependent apoptosis pathway that also functions in resolving the corpus luteum in this model.
evidence: This is speculation based on the differential caspase-3 levels in different knockouts.

claim: Most of the corpus luteum involution induced by PGF2α is through the RIPK3-RIPK1/FADD/caspase-8 pathway triggered by RIPK3 induction and phosphorylation at serine 165/threonine 166.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrated that most of the corpus luteum involution induced by PGF2α is through the RIPK3-RIPK1/FADD/caspase-8 pathway triggered by RIPK3 induction and phosphorylation at serine 165/threonine 166.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on all the genetic and biochemical data.

claim: The apoptotic role of RIPK3 has been observed ever since RIPK3 was first identified.
source: The apoptotic role of RIPK3 has been observed ever since RIPK3 was first identified (Sun et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as historical context with citation.

claim: Initial characterization of RIPK3 by ectopic overexpression indicated that it functioned in apoptosis.
source: The initial characterization of RIPK3, mainly by ectopic overexpression, indicated that it functioned in apoptosis (Sun et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as historical context with citation.

claim: RIPK3 was later identified as a key signaling molecule for necroptosis due to its ability to specifically phosphorylate MLKL.
source: Later, however, RIPK3 was identified as a key signaling molecule for necroptosis due to its ability to specifically phosphorylate MLKL, the executioner of this form of cell death (Cho et al., 2009; He et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2009; Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as historical context with citations.

claim: The mutation-induced change of RIPK3 function from pro-necroptotic to apoptotic most likely mimicked the specific phosphorylation at the serine 164 site.
source: We now propose that this mutation-induced change of RIPK3 function from pro-necroptotic to apoptotic most likely mimicked the specific phosphorylation at the serine 164 (mouse 165) site.
evidence: This is a proposal/conclusion based on the data presented.

claim: Serine 164 amide nitrogen forms a conserved H-bond with the carbonyl oxygen of phenylalanine 160.
source: The serine 164 amide nitrogen forms a conserved H-bond with the carbonyl oxygen of phenylalanine 160 (part of the DFG motif of kinase), a feature important to maintain the RIPK3 active configuration (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Introducing a phosphate group at serine 164 disrupts the critical interaction with phenylalanine 160, resulting in loss of RIPK3 kinase function.
source: Introducing a phosphate group at this site conceivably disrupts this critical interaction, resulting in loss of function of the RIPK3 kinase and a conformational change that allows the RHIM domain to be available for RHIM-RHIM interaction between RIPK3 and RIPK1.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on structural knowledge and experimental data.

claim: RIPK1 protein functions as an adaptor for the recruitment of FADD and caspase-8 in RIPK3-mediated apoptosis.
source: Interestingly, RIPK1 protein functions here purely as an adaptor for the recruitment of FADD and caspase-8, and its kinase activity is not required for this apoptosis function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing RIPK1 kinase inhibitors don't block this pathway.

claim: RIPK1 kinase activity is not required for RIPK3-mediated apoptosis function.
source: Interestingly, RIPK1 protein functions here purely as an adaptor for the recruitment of FADD and caspase-8, and its kinase activity is not required for this apoptosis function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing RIPK1 kinase inhibitors don't block this pathway.

claim: The apoptosis-inducing activity of RIPK1 initiated by RIPK3 phosphorylation is not sensitive to RIPK1 kinase inhibitors.
source: Therefore, unlike the apoptosis and necroptosis-inducing functions of RIPK1 when it responds to the activation of the TNF receptor family of proteins, the apoptosis-inducing activity of RIPK1 that is initiated by RIPK3 phosphorylation is not sensitive to RIPK1 kinase inhibitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the inhibitor data.

claim: The phosphorylation of serine 164/threonine 165 is likely catalyzed by RIPK3 itself.
source: Although we cannot completely rule out the possibility of another yet to be identified kinase(s) that carries out the phosphorylation of serine 164/threonine 165 of RIPK3, our current data favor the idea that the phosphorylation is catalyzed by RIPK3 itself.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinase-dead mutant data.

claim: RIPK3 naturally has dual roles in both necroptosis and apoptosis.
source: Our investigation has now clearly shown that RIPK3 naturally has dual roles in both necroptosis and apoptosis.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study based on all the data.

claim: In cells where RIPK3 kinase predominantly signals to necroptosis, the RIPK3 chaperone Hsp90/CDC37 level is relatively high.
source: In cells in which the RIPK3 kinase predominantly signals to necroptosis, like in human colon cancer HT29 cells, the RIPK3 chaperone Hsp90/CDC37 level is relatively high
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 4A.

claim: High Hsp90/CDC37 levels allow RIPK3 to fold into a configuration that can only be activated by upstream signaling molecules.
source: which allows RIPK3 to fold into a configuration that can only be activated by upstream signaling molecules, be that either RIPK1 in response to TNF receptor family members, or TRIF and ZBP1/DAI in response to toll-like receptors or Z-RNA, respectively.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on the chaperone data.

claim: In cells with high Hsp90/CDC37, RIPK3 kinase activity is silent before upstream activation signals arrive.
source: In this case, RIPK3 kinase activity is silent, and no auto-phosphorylation signal or downstream substrate MLKL phosphorylation occurs before upstream activation signals arrive.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a mechanistic explanation.

claim: In cells with low Hsp90/CDC37 chaperone level, newly generated RIPK3 can auto-phosphorylate its serine 164/threonine 165 sites.
source: However, in cells in which Hsp90/CDC37 chaperone level is relatively low or artificially inhibited by Hsp90 inhibitors or knocked down by the specific shRNA, the newly generated RIPK3, either by artificial induction (through transient transfection or Dox-induced expression) or by physiological signals like PGF2α, can auto-phosphorylate its serine 164/threonine 165 sites of its conserved kinase activation loop, triggering apoptosis through the RIPK3-RIPK1-FADD-caspase-8 pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mice bearing phospho-mimic mutations S165D/T166E showed spontaneous activation of apoptosis in all RIPK3-expressing tissues.
source: Consistently, mice bearing the phospho-mimic mutations of these sites (S165D/T166E) showed spontaneous activation of apoptosis in all RIPK3-expressing tissues, including lung, intestines, and spleen, and these mice die within a month after birth.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Whether the apoptotic events in S165D/T166E knock-in mouse tissues are caused by activation of the RIPK1-FADD-caspase-8 pathway still requires genetic verification.
source: However, whether the apoptotic events observed in those S165D/T166E knock-in mouse tissues are caused by the activation of the RIPK1-FADD-caspase-8 pathway still requires genetic verification.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation/future direction in the Discussion.

claim: If the apoptosis in S165D/T166E mice is through RIPK1-FADD-caspase-8 pathway, knocking out either caspase-8 or FADD gene should rescue the phenotype.
source: if indeed the case, knocking out either caspase-8 or FADD gene in those mice should rescue the phenotype.
evidence: This is a prediction/speculation about future experiments.

claim: The chaperone level of Hsp90/CDC37 relative to RIPK3 is important to dictate the necroptotic or apoptotic function of mouse RIPK3.
source: The chaperone level of Hsp90/CDC37 relative to RIPK3 is important to dictate the necroptotic or apoptotic function of mouse RIPK3 as well.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by mouse cell data.

claim: Serine 164/threonine 165 phosphorylation of RIPK3 is a unique biomarker for RIPK3-mediated apoptosis pathway.
source: Serine 164/threonine 165 phosphorylation of RIPK3 seems to be a unique biomarker for this RIPK3-mediated apoptosis pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the antibody specificity.

claim: The anti-phospho-S164/T165 monoclonal antibody should be useful to identify tissues and cells in which RIPK3-mediated apoptosis pathway is activated.
source: Our development of a monoclonal antibody that specifically recognizes this phosphorylation event should be useful to identify tissues and cells in which this pathway is activated.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the utility of the antibody.

evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: An analog of PGF2α was able to induce the expression of S165/T166 phosphorylated RIPK3 and apoptosis in primary granulosa cells from ovaries of young wild-type mice.
source: and indeed, an analog of PGF2α was able to induce the expression of S165/T166 phosphorylated RIPK3 and apoptosis in the primary granulosa cells from ovaries of young wild-type mice (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: DT could not induce apoptosis and luteum resolution in the ovary of PGF receptor knockout, RIPK3 knockout, FADD/MLKL double knockout, and Ripk3S165A-T166A/S165A-T166A knock-in mice.
source: However, DT could not induce apoptosis and luteum resolution in the ovary of PGF receptor knockout, RIPK3 knockout, FADD/MLKL double knockout, and Ripk3S165A-T166A/S165A-T166A knock-in mice, confirming this intracellular pathway of apoptosis in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 7F-G.

claim: The serine 165/threonine 166 phospho-RIPK3 signal only naturally appears in luteal granulosa cells when mice reach a certain age.
source: Although the RIPK3-mediated apoptosis can be recapitulated in this hyper-ovulation model using an agonist (DT) of PGF2α in young mice, the serine 165/threonine 166 phospho-RIPK3 signal only naturally appears in luteal granulosa cells when mice reach a certain age.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: RIPK3 knockout and Ripk3S165A-T166A/S165A-T166A knock-in mice do not show any fertility defect in their normal reproductive age.
source: The RIPK3 knockout and Ripk3S165A-T166A/S165A-T166A knock-in mice do not show any fertility defect in their normal reproductive age

claim: The PGF2α-induced, RIPK3-mediated apoptotic pathway does not have a critical role in luteum resolution during the normal reproductive cycle when mice are young.
source: indicating that the PGF2α-induced, RIPK3-mediated apoptotic pathway does not have a critical role in luteum resolution during the normal reproductive cycle when the mice are young.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of fertility defects in knockout mice.

claim: The RIPK3-mediated apoptotic pathway may have a specific role during mouse ovary aging when all corpora lutea eventually become albicans.
source: It is thus interesting to speculate that such a pathway may have a specific role during mouse ovary aging when all corpora lutea eventually become albicans.
